clue.text: Good lord, that's Agatha taking a turn on the ski slope

definitions.text: a turn on the ski slope

blocks.note: the exclamation read as the name of the Lord
i.e. stands for id est, 'that is'

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims in surprise at seeing Agatha make a turn while skiing.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is defined twice: as the surname of the crime writer Agatha, and as the skiing term for a swinging turn, also spelt christy.
explanation.definitionFit: Agatha Christie wrote detective novels, and a christie is a high-speed parallel swing used by skiers to change direction.

clue.text: Play it again in snub for Picasso, say

indicators.note: these words are placed inside the word that follows

blocks.note: bis is the call for an encore, asking for a piece to be repeated
to cut someone is to snub them

explanation.surface: A request to hear a tune again, made in a rude manner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Play it again' evokes Casablanca; bis is Latin for twice, shouted as an encore. 'Say' marks Picasso as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Picasso founded Cubism with Braque, so he is an example of an artist of that movement.

clue.text: Fleece that is very new

definitions.note: the answer is a noun for a person who is very new

blocks.note: to rook someone is to fleece or swindle them
i.e. is the abbreviation for 'that is'

explanation.surface: A sheep's coat described as brand new.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fleece' looks like wool; it is the verb meaning to cheat.
explanation.definitionFit: A rookie is a novice or recruit in their first season, someone very new to a job.

clue.text: A Nash girl depicted making imaginary pass

definitions.note: Shangri-La is the imaginary paradise valley of Lost Horizon, reached over a Himalayan pass

indicators.note: something depicted is portrayed in a new form, so the letters are rendered differently

blocks.note: the three words supply the letters

explanation.surface: A portrait of a girl by the painter Nash, shown making an imaginary gesture.
explanation.walkthrough: Shangri-La is the hidden Himalayan utopia in James Hilton's novel Lost Horizon.
explanation.definitionFit: Shangri-La is a fictional paradise in a remote Tibetan mountain valley, an imaginary place.

clue.text: Peruvian stock too hot to handle

blocks.note: the Incas were the ancient people of Peru
your stock is your ancestry or descent

explanation.surface: A Peruvian product that is too risky to deal in.
explanation.definitionFit: Incandescent means glowing with heat, so hot that nothing could be held or touched.

clue.text: Society at best is hilarious

definitions.note: the answer is a noun; 'is hilarious' equals 'is a scream'

blocks.note: S is the standard abbreviation for society
the cream is the best part of anything

explanation.surface: A remark that high society at its finest is very funny.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that is a scream is extremely funny, so the noun stands in for hilarious after 'is'.

clue.text: A cockney's mate in the country

blocks.note: first meaning: in rhyming slang '... plate' means mate, shortened to the first word
second meaning: the large nation in East Asia

explanation.surface: A Londoner's friend living out in the countryside.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockney rhyming slang, from East London, replaces a word with a rhyming phrase and then drops the rhyme: china plate, mate.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both the slang term for a friend and the name of the most populous Asian nation.

clue.text: Exotic, in the improved state

indicators.note: improved means altered for the better, so the letters are reworked

blocks.note: the two words supply letters
Cal. is an abbreviation for the US state of California

explanation.surface: Something exotic presented as being in better condition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Improved state' reads as one phrase but improved works only on the two words before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Ethnical, an older form of ethnic, describes cultures seen as foreign, hence exotic to the speaker.

clue.text: Some hot stuff said to have assembled

indicators.note: said means spoken, so the word is judged by its sound

blocks.note: mustard is a hot condiment

explanation.surface: A rumour that some spicy goods have been collected together.
explanation.definitionFit: Troops are mustered when they are gathered together for inspection, so the word means assembled.

clue.text: Keeping up? You can by going round

indicators.note: letters going round are spun about and come out in a new order

blocks.note: the three words supply the letters

explanation.surface: Someone asks if you are keeping pace, and suggests you can manage by circling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keeping up' sounds like keeping pace with others; here it means staying afloat.
explanation.definitionFit: Buoyancy is the upward force or tendency that keeps a floating object from sinking, so it is literally keeping things up.

clue.text: Blues numbers, perhaps

blocks.note: surface reading: songs in the blues style
setter's reading: Blues are Oxford and Cambridge sportsmen, and their rowing crews are of a certain number of oarsmen

explanation.surface: A guess at what some tunes from a blues set might be.
explanation.walkthrough: A Blue is someone who has represented Oxford or Cambridge; the Boat Race crews row in boats of eight, called eights, and eight is also a number.
explanation.definitionFit: Eights are racing boats with eight rowers, as used by university crews, and the plural of a number too.

clue.text: Hack, after a swig of beer, gets a punch

indicators.note: one piece is set after another, so it comes second

blocks.note: a draught is a swallow of drink, and draught beer is drawn from the cask
a hack is a horse for ordinary riding

explanation.surface: A journalist who has had a beer gets thumped in a pub brawl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hack' wants to be a journalist and 'punch' a blow; a Suffolk Punch is a breed of heavy farm horse.
explanation.definitionFit: The Suffolk Punch is a breed of heavy farm horse used for pulling loads, so a punch is one example.

clue.text: Do some of your best in goal

indicators.note: only some of the letters of the following words are used, sitting together

blocks.note: the letters run across best, in and goal

explanation.surface: An encouragement to a goalkeeper to perform well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Do' here is the slang verb for swindle, not the everyday 'perform'.
explanation.definitionFit: To sting someone is slang for cheating them out of money, just as to do someone means to con them.

clue.text: River rodent in simple story

indicators.note: these words are placed inside the word that follows

blocks.note: R is the map abbreviation for river
a rat is a rodent
naive means simple or unsophisticated

explanation.surface: A simple tale about a rodent living by a river, like The Wind in the Willows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Simple story' looks like the definition, but simple belongs to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A narrative is an account of connected events, which is what a story is.

clue.text: Financial agreement  to let prize-winner's money include half a dance

indicators.note: to include something is to hold it within, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: to hire out is to let
a purse is the prize money in a boxing match or race
half of the cha-cha

explanation.surface: A deal letting a prize-winner's cash cover dancing lessons.
explanation.walkthrough: A purse is the money put up for a contest. Hire purchase is the British term for buying goods by instalments.
explanation.definitionFit: Hire purchase is a credit arrangement where goods are paid for in instalments, a kind of financial agreement.

clue.text: Caught the beast in drug plant

blocks.note: c is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught
the eland is a large African antelope, a crossword favourite beast
taken as written
E is slang for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: An animal arrested while high on narcotics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drug plant' looks like a single phrase for the definition; only plant defines.
explanation.definitionFit: The celandine is a small wild flowering plant, with yellow star-shaped blooms in early spring.

clue.text: Not potable, but are wet as can be

indicators.note: can be suggests what the letters could become once moved around

blocks.note: the three words supply the letters

explanation.surface: A comment on some liquid: undrinkable, yet as wet as can be.
explanation.walkthrough: 'As wet as can be' reads as an idiom, but as is fodder and can be the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Water from the ocean is too salty to drink, so it is the classic example of water that is not potable.

clue.text: Ship's doctor takes time to fish

indicators.note: to take something in is to hold it, so one piece goes inside

blocks.note: T is the abbreviation for time
a ship's medical officer is called its surgeon

explanation.surface: A naval medic pauses to go angling.
explanation.definitionFit: The sturgeon is a large fish of northern waters, prized as the source of caviar.

clue.text: Captivate Sir Peter in the foyer

blocks.note: to entrance is to captivate
Sir Peter Hall, the theatre director who founded the RSC

explanation.surface: A theatre director charming the audience in the theatre lobby.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Peter Hall was a celebrated British theatre director, founder of the Royal Shakespeare Company.
explanation.definitionFit: An entrance hall is the room just inside the front door of a building, the same as a foyer.

clue.text: It removes, if soldiers are around

indicators.note: things that are around something stand on either side of it
turned around means facing the other way, so read backwards

blocks.note: the Royal Engineers, RE, taken twice since soldiers is plural, one lot for each side
as, as in 'as it were', can mean if

explanation.surface: A thing that clears away, but only when the troops are nearby.
explanation.walkthrough: Loose wordplay: soldiers (two lots of Royal Engineers, reversed) are on both sides of the word for if.
explanation.definitionFit: An eraser is a rubber, the tool that removes pencil marks, so it is something that removes.

clue.text: Pass up the French composer

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the letters read from bottom to top

blocks.note: to hand something over is to pass it
le is French for the

explanation.surface: Someone declines to play the French composer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pass up' looks like the phrase meaning decline, but up acts only on the French article.
explanation.definitionFit: George Frideric Handel was the German-born Baroque composer of Messiah and Water Music.

clue.text: Artisan's counter-occupation with the judge's seat

blocks.note: your work is your occupation
the bench is where a judge sits

explanation.surface: A craftsman's job set against a judge's position.
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphen in 'counter-occupation' is a fake join: counter ends the definition and occupation starts the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A workbench is the sturdy table at which a craftsman does manual work, a counter for the trade.

clue.text: Beat interrupting live rap

indicators.note: something interrupting breaks into the middle of another

blocks.note: to lam is to thrash or beat
to be is to exist, to live

explanation.surface: A rhythm cutting into a live rap music performance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beat' and 'rap' suggest music; rap is the blame you take, as in 'take the rap'.
explanation.definitionFit: Taking the rap means accepting the blame or punishment, so the rap is the blame.

clue.text: A girl almost ordinary

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter is left off

blocks.note: normal means ordinary

explanation.surface: A description of a young woman as pretty much average.
explanation.definitionFit: Norma is a female first name, and crosswords routinely define given names as a girl.

clue.text: Prohibition after the ancient Greek

indicators.note: one piece is set after another, so it comes second

blocks.note: taken as written
a ban is a prohibition

explanation.surface: A ban imposed following the rule of some Greek of old.
explanation.definitionFit: A Theban was a citizen of Thebes, a powerful city-state of classical Greece.

clue.text: A striped comic moseyed along

indicators.note: something comic is a funny, distorted version, so the letters are mangled

blocks.note: the two words supply the letters

explanation.surface: A clown in a stripy costume ambled about.
explanation.definitionFit: To traipse is to walk wearily or aimlessly, much as moseying is a slow aimless stroll.

clue.text: A look-alike, sometimes dead

blocks.note: the definition proper: someone who closely resembles another
a hint at the idiom in which the word is often preceded by dead

explanation.surface: A double who, eerily, is now and then deceased.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'dead ringer' is an exact double; 'dead' here means exact, not deceased.
explanation.definitionFit: A ringer is a person or horse that closely resembles another, especially one substituted fraudulently.

clue.text: Brainy brother tucking into a healthy breakfast

indicators.note: something tucking into food goes inside it, so one piece sits within the other

blocks.note: Br is the abbreviation for brother
cereal is a wholesome breakfast

explanation.surface: A clever sibling eating a nourishing morning meal.
explanation.definitionFit: Cerebral relates to the brain and describes someone intellectual, which is what brainy means.
